SAMPLING · FIELD NOTES

How to Compare Test Pans Without Fooling Yourself

By the Old-Timer · Published October 7, 2026

The Old-Timer is Gold Trails’ editorial voice. Content assembled with assistance from ChatGPT. Sources are linked throughout.

You have two pans in front of you. One shows a bright little flake; the other shows several smaller specks. Which spot deserves another sample? Before choosing, ask a quieter question: did you give both spots a fair test?

This article offers a practical notebook routine for recreational prospecting. It is an editorial recommendation, not a laboratory method or a way to establish a mineral reserve. For choosing your first locations, start with Where Gold Settles in a River.

The short version

  • Keep the starting amount and processing method consistent.
  • Record the location and sediment layer, not just the nearest landmark.
  • Separate confirmed gold from particles you have not identified.
  • Repeat promising results and retain disappointing results in your notes.
  • Use the comparison to choose your next sample, not to promise a day’s earnings.

Decide what you are comparing

A comparison needs a clear question. “Which of these three accessible gravel positions should I investigate next?” is manageable. “How rich is this whole river?” asks far more than a few recreational pans can establish.

Try changing one thing at a time. If you compare an inside-bar surface sample with deeper material from a bedrock pocket, you have changed both position and layer. That may be useful exploration, but record the difference. It is not a clean test of whether inside bends outperform bedrock.

Give each sample an identity before panning: A1, A2, B1, and so on. Use the letter for a location or layer and the number for a separate sample. A label is a small defense against remembering your favorite result as the only result.

Start with a comparable amount

A nearly empty pan and a heaped pan are different starting points. Use a marked container or scoop, and choose whether you will measure material before or after screening. Stick with that choice through the comparison.

Neither choice magically makes a sample representative. Measuring before screening describes the starting gravel; measuring after screening describes the screened fraction. They answer different questions. Write down the screen opening as well, and do not silently switch between the two.

Keep layers separate when possible. If you combine surface gravel and material from a compact seam, you cannot later assign the result to either layer. A note such as “mixed layers; exploratory sample” is more useful than a false impression of precision.

Keep your recovery method steady

Use the same pan, screening approach, and basic technique for the samples you want to compare. Avoid overloading, and give yourself enough time to finish each pan carefully. If the method changes halfway through, mark the change instead of pretending the results are interchangeable.

The Forest Service and BLM panning booklet describes separating lighter material from the heavier fraction and checking oversized material before discarding it. That check is a useful reminder that the contents you see at the finish are a recovery result, not a perfect inventory of everything you started with. Gold Panning · 2018 revisionU.S. Forest Service & BLMPrinted pages 10–11 · PDF pages 14–15Describes panning technique and checking oversized material before discarding it. Regional guidance is not a mineral-resource assessment.View original source ↗Opens another website in a new tab; this article stays open.

If you spill a pan or lose track of a label, keep the note but flag that result as compromised. Do not enter a zero for a sample you did not successfully process. Zero recovered, not examined, and lost sample are three different observations.

Know what you are counting

A yellow flash deserves attention, but it does not settle identification. USGS names pyrite, chalcopyrite, and weathered mica among the common gold look-alikes. It describes gold deforming under a metal point, whereas those look-alikes may crumble, powder, or flake. What is “Fool’s Gold?”U.S. Geological SurveyMineral identification FAQIdentifies pyrite, chalcopyrite, and weathered mica as gold look-alikes, and describes differences in their physical behavior.View original source ↗Opens another website in a new tab; this article stays open.

For a tiny particle you cannot examine confidently, write “suspected gold” and preserve it for a closer look. A blurry phone photograph or a flash of sunlight is not a dependable substitute for identification. You do not need to force an answer at the river.

Keep particle counts separate from mass. Five very small flakes do not necessarily outweigh one larger piece. If you have not weighed the recovered gold with suitable equipment, leave mass blank. A blank field is more truthful than an estimate presented as a measurement.

Repeat the promising spot—and remember the others

One unusually large particle can dominate a small sample. The Yukon report catalog describes the difficulty of sampling placer gravel when the presence or absence of a single gold particle changes the result. Its subject is placer drilling; it supports the general caution about small samples, not a claim that a particular number of hand pans is enough. An Evaluation of the Gold Recovery of Placer Drills Using Radio Tracers (Part II)Government of Yukon · Open Government CanadaReport catalog · sampling limitationsExplains how inclusion or loss of a single gold particle can strongly affect a small sample. The report concerns placer drilling, not a validated hand-panning protocol.View original source ↗Opens another website in a new tab; this article stays open.

Our suggested next step is to take a separate repeat sample from the promising position, using the same starting measure and method. Keep both results visible in your notebook. If the first was exciting and the second disappointing, that disagreement is part of the story.

There is no honest universal rule that two pans, five pans, or ten pans prove a deposit. Sample size, grain distribution, recovery, and the question you are asking all matter. A professional evaluation needs a designed sampling program. Your recreational notebook can still help you make a better-informed choice about where to spend the next hour.

A notebook you can actually use

Record enough detail that tomorrow’s you can understand today’s decision. These are suggested fields, not mandatory reporting requirements.

  • Sample: unique label, date, position description, and sediment layer.
  • Input: measured amount, unit, before/after screening, and screen opening.
  • Processing: equipment, technique changes, spills, or other problems.
  • Observation: confirmed or suspected gold, particle count and size notes, and measured mass only when available.
  • Decision: repeat, test nearby, review identification, or move on—and why.

Download a blank sample log (CSV). It opens in spreadsheet software; it contains no example findings or invented measurements.

For example: “B2; gravel resting on exposed rock; one level marked scoop before screening; same equipment as B1; one suspected fine flake; repeat after identification check.” This is a fictional entry showing the level of detail, not a reported discovery.

Let the notes guide a modest decision

At the end of a short comparison, ask what you can reasonably say: “This position gave me repeatable recovered gold under today’s method,” or “The result was uncertain and needs another test.” Avoid turning either statement into an estimate of the river’s total gold or the value of a claim.

Check access and local rules before sampling. Stay with safely accessible material, avoid unstable banks and boulders, and do not enter dangerous water to keep a comparison going. You can finish a notebook tomorrow; there is no need to finish it at any cost today.

A good test pan does not have to be full of gold. It has to leave you knowing a little more than you knew before.
